                    ### Question
                    An 80-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after the sudden onset of sub-sternal chest pain and shortness of breath while sitting in a chair. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 42 years. Four days after admission, he becomes tachycardic and then loses consciousness; the cardiac monitor shows irregular electrical activity. Cardiac examination shows a new systolic murmur at the apex. Despite appropriate measures, he dies. Microscopic evaluation of the myocardium is most likely to show which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Coagulative necrosis with dense neutrophilic infiltrate
opb. Wavy myocardial fibers without inflammatory cells
opc. Low cellularity with dense, non-contractile scar tissue
opd. Dense granulation tissue with collagenous scar formation
ope. Hyperemic granulation tissue with abundance of macrophages

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):

Given his risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, and extensive smoking history), myocardial necrosis is expected. The development of tachycardia and loss of consciousness indicates severe myocardial damage, which aligns with the presence of coagulative necrosis. The new systolic murmur suggests possible structural changes due to myocardial damage, further supporting the likelihood of coagulative necrosis with dense neutrophilic infiltrate, which is typical in the early stages of myocardial infarction. Therefore, the most likely microscopic finding in this case is coagulative necrosis with dense neutrophilic infiltrate, corroborated by the consensus that acute myocardial infarction leads to this type of necrosis.
